 TV Review: ‘Nocturne’ is a Twisted Psychological Thriller with a Killer Who’s Just as Dangerous Behind Bars
 by 
 Steven Prusakowski 
 November 18, 2026, 2:11 pm 
 The best crime thrillers are the ones that keep you guessing, revealing just enough to keep you hooked while holding back the answers you’re desperate to uncover. The most compelling characters often work the same way, with far more going on beneath the surface than they initially let on. If you’re looking for a psychological thriller that leads you down that path of intrigue, Apple TV’s series Nocturne is a prime suspect. It’s a psychological puzzle with something far more disturbing waiting around every corner.
 Intrigue is the psychological space between what we know and what we want to know. And living in that space is where Nocturne thrives. It possesses a strong noir vibe, led by Liev Schreiber as a dark, brooding anti-hero, a man of few words whose hazy past and inner turmoil tell a much bigger story than he lets on. Like the world he lives in, there’s always something lurking beneath the surface. It’s that mystery, combined with an unsettling core element so disturbing that you’ll want to know what’s behind the next door.
 Based on The Sandman and Lazarus , two novels by Lars Kepler, the pen name of Swedish husband-and-wife writing team Alexandra Coelho Ahndoril and Alexander Ahndoril , Nocturne follows Jonah ( Schreiber ), an ex-soldier and former homicide detective from the Philadelphia PD who is pulled back into a case with a personal connection. Jurek Walter, played by Stephen Graham , is a serial killer whose presence continues to haunt Jonah, even from behind the walls of a psychiatric hospital. When Michael, a boy connected to Jurek’s past, returns after years of being presumed dead, disturbing questions arise. His sister is still missing, and even while Jurek is behind bars, the killer’s influence seems to reach far beyond the walls of his cell.
 The 10-episode season’s pacing is a bit slow at first, but like a novel, it can take a little while to connect with the story as you get to know the characters and the world they’re inhabiting. Nocturne does not throw a lot at you at once. Rather, it keeps pulling you in little by little. Honestly, after the first episode, I wasn’t quite sure it was going to click with me, but I trusted the cast to win me over. Schreiber, Beetz, and Camp are some of my favorite actors working today. So I pushed through, and I’m glad I did. With each episode, the intrigue grew. I’m not saying it was boring in any way, but the slow-reveal approach I praise is also something that will challenge some viewers in these days of instant gratification.
 The characters start off as strangers to the audience and don’t provide much exposition right away. Instead, we’re given a trail of breadcrumbs. As we get to know them, we realize there’s far more going on than initially meets the eye. Each character reveals only what they want us to see, whether they’re trying to accomplish something or hide something. That’s part of the fun. We don’t know who’s harboring secrets, what’s motivating them, or how the various pieces of this web will eventually connect.
 The lead performances are top-notch. Schreiber’s Jonah is a man of few words, but his pain can be read on his face in everything he says and does. We know that he has suffered a loss, but it’s not until a few episodes in that we realize why it burns so deep inside him. He’s a tough, rough-around-the-edges type who uses his pain like a shield, protecting him from emotional connections. His relationship with Saga is the one weakness and gives the series an emotional center, with Jonah’s protectiveness matched by Saga’s determination. They clearly care about each other, even if neither is particularly good at showing it.
 The biggest surprise is Zazie Beetz , who’s excellent in a dual role of sorts. She plays Saga, an FBI agent on the case and Jonah’s surrogate daughter, who goes undercover as a patient to get closer to the serial killer on his own ground. While Jurek is locked away, she’s the one choosing to enter his world. Like Jonah, there’s more to her than meets the eye, and that becomes even more apparent when she takes on the identity of Esther. Beetz excels at playing a character who is herself playing another character, adding unexpected layers to her performance. As Saga, she’s determined and driven by her instincts, but as Esther, she’s more guarded and carefully calculating. Watching Beetz navigate those two sides, sometimes within the same scene, is particularly impressive – never revealing who is on the other side of the walls she has built. At times, I questioned where Esther ends and where Saga begins. Seven episodes in, I still don’t know. She’s fantastic.
 Then there’s the killer, Jurek Walter, played by Graham. The actor is quite the chameleon, and you see it here again. As I mentioned to him during my interview (you can watch below), I’ve been watching his work for decades, but never knew the actor was Scottish until I heard him accept his Emmy. Whether he’s playing the intimidating Al Capone in Boardwalk Empire or the heartbroken father in Adolescence , he transforms completely. And in Nocturne , he’s unrecognizable once again, not only throughout the series but often from scene to scene.
 Jurek is another character hidden behind walls, this time both physical and psychological. He’s a sadistic killer locked up in a high-security psychiatric facility. Stripped of his freedom, his only remaining weapons are his smarts, his charm, and his voice. Jurek’s voice and personality are never quite consistent, changing with every person he interacts with to get what he can from each relationship. He’s like a snake charmer, playing just the tune needed to seduce each person in the room. Like the great Hannibal Lecter of The Silence of the Lambs , Jurek is a brilliant and terrifying man whose ability to stay ahead of everyone and manipulate those around him makes him incredibly dangerous. Even behind bars, Jurek Walter is the most dangerous person in the room.
 Watching him and Saga face off is one of the series’ most thrilling elements. Even though almost all of their communication is limited to talking through a prison toilets, it somehow stays incredibly intense. It’s a high-stakes chess match, with each trying to anticipate the other’s next move, even though neither will admit the game they are playing. It’s a twisted game of psychological cat and mouse where nobody is quite who they seem. Saga walks a dangerous line, not only to succeed in her mission, but to survive. As I watched, I found myself begging her not to go through with whatever crazy scheme she was about to attempt, only to watch her do it just about every time, putting herself in even more danger than expected and neccessary.
 One of the people who seems to be under Jurek’s spell is the prison guard, Karl, played by Rory Culkin . Culkin makes you question both the appeal Jurek holds over him and Karl’s own motives, adding another interesting layer to the story. What is it that makes him willing to strike up a friendship with Jurek? Is there more beneath the surface? Again, I still do not know.
 The supporting cast is equally strong, including Chrissy Metz and the incredible Bill Camp . Camp has never given a bad performance, as far as I’m concerned, and always has me wishing I had more time with his character. No exception here. Metz fits right in, taking on much darker territory as the mother of a missing child.
 The series definitely has a similar feel to Task , probably because of its Pennsylvania setting, but also due to its FBI procedural elements, small-town atmosphere, and the lone-wolf detective back on a case he can’t leave alone. Both shows use their Pennsylvania settings to create a gritty, lived-in world populated with people carrying plenty of personal baggage. The difference is that Nocturne leans more heavily into psychological manipulation and the cat-and-mouse games between its lead detective, undercover agent, and imprisoned killer. This isn’t a series for anyone who wants to know everything up front. Patience is required. But after screening seven episodes, I’ve been thoroughly engaged and always anticipating what’s next.
 Those looking for a more grounded, procedural crime drama like Zodiac or a deeply moving, socially timely show like Furious ( read my review ) may be disappointed. Nocturne has plenty to keep your interest, but perhaps not as much that will resonate long after the credits roll. Instead, it gives us an intriguing tale, characters who feel like puzzles, and a fun watch that keeps turning the pages, even if it all becomes a little convoluted at times. There are some big questions you may not want to dwell on, and moments when thinking too hard about the details could pull you out of its spell. Honestly, sometimes not knowing the answers is half the fun.
 It is quite dark at times and does not paint a pretty picture of the world. The idea behind this killer’s methods is about as demented as it comes. He keeps his victims alive and buried with food and water, prolonging their torture for as long as possible. That’s especially disturbing when you consider that two of his victims are kids. Peeling back the layers of this psychological onion is a deeply unsettling experience. The deeper you go, the more disturbing the truth becomes.
 Nocturne is a pulse-pounding, heart-racing puzzle, with a cast of characters compelling enough to keep you invested. Peeling back its layers is like opening a door you know you shouldn’t, only to discover something even more disturbing waiting on the other side. Will it all pay off after 10 episodes? We shall see. It’s difficult to land these things, but I’m excited to find out if they do.
 Check out Nocturne on Apple TV and my interviews with the cast below, which are 99.5% spoiler-free, especially if you’ve watched the several episodes.
